notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material for most verses. I couldn't search further, so some areas are missing:
- I have nothing from netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org (modern scholarship), from Lutheran, Pentecostal-denominational or Orthodox sites, or on prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace readings. Those are left out.
- Augustine's exposition (newadvent.org) follows the Latin numbering, so it calls this psalm "Psalm 80" in its verse links.

**Whole psalm / setting**
- Guzik says it was probably sung at the Feast of Tabernacles. That feast remembered the wilderness journey and included reading the law aloud, so the psalm is a call to renew the covenant.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/
- Matthew Henry sees two purposes for public worship here: to give glory to God (vv. 1–7) and to be taught by Him (vv. 8–16).  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_081.cfm

**v. 1**
- Gill says God is Israel's "strength" because His mighty arm brought them out of Egypt, kept them in the wilderness and settled them in Canaan. He also gives every true believer strength to bear trials and keep going to the end.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-81.html
- Spurgeon wants loud, whole-hearted singing from the whole congregation. He would rather hear rough, untrained singing than miss hearty praise.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/
- Catholic (Augustine): "Asaph" means "congregation," so the psalm is addressed to the baptized Church. Where words fail, believers should still rejoice aloud.  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801081.htm

**v. 2**
- Boice, citing Delitzsch: v. 1 calls the whole congregation, v. 2 the Levite musicians, and v. 3 the priests who blew the trumpets. VanGemeren takes the tambourine as a sign that people danced.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/
- Augustine reads it as an allegory. The psalm (spiritual) and the tambourine, made of animal hide (fleshly), mean that people who receive spiritual things should give material things back, such as practical help and gifts. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801081.htm

**v. 3**
- Gill: the New Moon may be the first day of the month Tishri, the Feast of Trumpets. Following De Dieu, he reads the second phrase as "full moon," pointing to Passover or Tabernacles. Spiritually, he sees the trumpet as a picture of gospel preaching.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-81.html
- Guzik: this trumpet called the people to gather for the feast. It was not one of the instruments accompanying the praise.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/
- Augustine: the New Moon stands for the new life in Christ (2 Cor 5:17), so the trumpet means preaching that new life boldly. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801081.htm

**v. 4** (where traditions differ)
- Gill: the feast was commanded by God, not made up by people. In the same way, Christ's gospel ordinances must be kept because God appointed them.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-81.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) uses this verse against church festivals God never commanded, such as Christmas and Whitsun. He tests every ritual by asking whether it is "a law of the God of Jacob."  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm
- Henry, quoted by Kidner, is softer: set times exist so that we can meet one another to praise God together.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/

**v. 5**
- "Joseph" stands for the whole nation. Spurgeon explains that in Egypt the people would have been known as Joseph's family.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm
- "Unfamiliar language", Henry's view: the Egyptian language, which made Israel's slavery worse because they lived as strangers in a strange land.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_081.cfm
- Gill's view: he weighs God's voice at Sinai and Moses' speech, but prefers the Egyptian language.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-81.html
- Spurgeon's view: God speaks as one with Israel. Egyptian was a foreign tongue in His worship, and in the sense of "I never knew you" He did not "know" Egypt's idolatry.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm
- Augustine: crossing the Red Sea pictures baptism. After it, believers come to understand mysteries in a "language" they did not know before.  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801081.htm

**v. 6**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the "basket" was the slaves' basket for carrying clay and bricks (Exod 1:14; 5:7).  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- Spurgeon: Israel did not win its freedom; it was a free gift of God's power. He sees a picture of the believer set free from slavery to the law and from trying to earn salvation.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm
- Gill also reads it as a picture of deliverance by Christ from sin, Satan and the law.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-81.html

**v. 7**
- Keil & Delitzsch: God answered from thunder-clouds, which both showed and hid Him, and struck Israel's enemies with lightning, mainly at the Red Sea. The psalm blends the two Meribah water stories. "Selah" marks a long musical pause.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- Spurgeon: Israel failed the test badly. "The story of Israel is only our own history in another shape."  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm
- Guzik: Meribah shows God training His people as well as rescuing them (Exod 17:1–7).  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/

**v. 8**
- Gill notes that "warn you" can be translated "testify against you," meaning against their complaining and idolatry.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-81.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: "if only" is a searching question that also expresses a longing wish.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- Kidner: God wants listeners as well as singers.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/

**v. 9**
- Keil & Delitzsch: this repeats the first of the Ten Commandments. They explain the difference between the two Hebrew words for "strange" and "foreign" god.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- Spurgeon applies it to Christians: the world, the flesh and the devil are foreign gods we must not bow to.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm

**v. 10** (where readings differ most)
- First half: Barnes says God's claim on Israel rests on the Exodus. It showed He alone is God, and it put Israel under obligation to Him.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- "Open wide": many writers see a picture of baby birds being fed (Barnes, Gill, Spurgeon). Gill takes it as wide-open prayer, praise, or hunger for spiritual food. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- Barnes limits the promise to real needs, of body or soul. God is able and willing to meet every "real necessity." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- Poole adds a condition: the promise is made "upon condition of your obedience." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- The Geneva Bible (Reformed) reads it as God rebuking Israel's unbelief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary goes furthest: God's gifts, temporal and spiritual, match how eagerly we long for them. Like Christ unable to do miracles where there was unbelief, God cannot give lavishly unless we desire largely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- Guzik and Maclaren: God fills whatever we open to Him, and our openness and expectation set the practical limit of what we receive.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/

**v. 11**
- Venema (in Spurgeon's notes): the Hebrew word suggests Israel "was not borne to me by a natural bent," like a ship without a favourable wind.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm
- Henry: they could have obeyed and were invited to; God was willing to be their God, but they would not be His people.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_081.cfm

**v. 12** (God's role in "giving them up")
- Calvinist-leaning writers quoted by Spurgeon: God withdraws His restraining grace and leaves people to their own corrupt wills. He supplies the power to act, but the evil comes from their own nature.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm
- Henry: God takes grace away only from those who have first thrown it away.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_081.cfm
- Matthew Henry's Concise: God is not the author of their sin; the blame is theirs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- The *Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary* (its tradition isn't stated) says God respects human moral freedom and will not force the will. People abandon God first, and then He lets them go their own way.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/81-15.html
- Guzik and Morgan: this is one of God's most severe judgments, letting people learn from the bitter results of their own folly.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-81/

**v. 13** (what God's "wish" means)
- Gill (Calvinist Baptist): the wish expresses what God commands and approves, not what He has purposed to happen, since no one can resist His purpose.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/81-13.html
- Clarke (Wesleyan) hears deep grief in the Hebrew, as if broken by sighs.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/81.htm
- The Homiletical commentary takes the wish as showing God's deep care for people.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/81-15.html

**v. 14**
- Spurgeon: sin takes away our armour; our enemies could never defeat us unless we first defeated ourselves.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps081.cfm
- Henry: "it is sin that makes our troubles long and salvation slow."  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_081.cfm
- Clarke: when God's promise seemed to fail, it was because Israel rejected His counsel.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/81.htm

**v. 15** (whose "time" lasts forever?)
- Most older Protestant writers say it is Israel's prosperity that would have lasted:
  - Clarke (Wesleyan)  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/81.htm
  - Wesley, "their happy time"  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/81-15.html
  - the Pulpit Commentary  same URL
  - Henry  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_081.cfm
- Gill records the other reading, from the Jewish commentators Rashi (Jarchi) and Ibn Ezra: the enemies' punishment lasts forever. He prefers Israel's happy state.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/81-15.html
- Augustine takes the enemies' reading ("Go into eternal fire").  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801081.htm The BSB's "their doom" also follows this reading.
- "Feign obedience": Trapp and the Pulpit Commentary note the Hebrew literally means "lied," meaning a forced or pretended submission.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/81-15.html

**v. 16**
- Gill: the finest wheat and the honey picture the gospel and Christ, the grain of wheat. The verse shows what Israel lost and what obedient believers enjoy.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-81.html
- Matthew Henry's Concise: Christ is the Bread of life and the Rock. Those who reject Him as Lord lose Him as Saviour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/81-10.htm
- Clarke notes that several Church Fathers read this verse as being about Christ. An old English paraphrase even reads the wheat as "the body of Criste."  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/81.htm
- Constable: the switch to "you" makes this a call to every later generation to follow God faithfully.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/81-15.html
- Guzik: the psalm ends sadly, on a missed opportunity.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-81.cfm
